segments.caption: The false positive paradox.
A test that's 99% accurate, a result that's usually wrong, 10,000 people to prove it, and why doctors always retest. Save this one!
A rare disease affects 1 in every 1,000 people.
You take a test that's 99% accurate. It comes back positive.
What's the chance you actually have the disease? Comment your guess before the answer.
Most people say 99%. Some say 90.
The real answer: about 9%. More than 9 out of 10 positive results are false alarms.
Here's how. Picture 10,000 people.
1 in 1,000 is sick, so 10 people really have the disease.
The test is 99% accurate, so it catches all 10 of them. 10 true positives.
But here's the twist. The other 9,990 people are healthy.
And the test is wrong for 1% of them. 1% of almost 10,000 is about 100 people.
100 healthy people told they're sick. Those are false positives.
Now count all the positives: 10 true, plus about 100 false. About 110.
Only 10 of those 110 are really sick. 10 divided by 110 is about 9%.
The trap is the base rate. The disease is so rare that the healthy crowd is huge.
A tiny error rate on a huge crowd creates more false alarms than there are real cases.
Ignoring how rare something is: that's called base rate neglect.
That's why doctors retest. Among the 110 positives, a second test clears almost all the false alarms.
After two positive tests, the chance you're really sick jumps to about 90%.
It's everywhere.
Your bank blocks your card for fraud, but it was just you shopping. Airport scanners beep at innocent bags. Spam filters bin real emails.
When the thing you're looking for is rare, most alarms are false.
So remember: a positive result depends on how rare the thing is, not just how accurate the test is.
Save this, and send it to someone who panics over every test result.
Your turn: if the disease affected 1 in 10 people instead, would a positive test be more or less trustworthy? Vote in the caption poll!
